title: Answering the Softer Letter
text:
In October 1962 American reconnaissance flights found Soviet nuclear missiles being installed in Cuba. President John F. Kennedy announced a naval quarantine of the island, and the world waited to see whether the superpowers would go to war.

On 26 October a long, emotional letter from Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev reached Washington. It suggested that the missiles could be removed if the United States promised not to invade Cuba. The next morning, before Washington had answered, Moscow radio broadcast a second, harder message: the Soviets now also demanded the removal of American Jupiter missiles from Turkey. That same day an American U-2 was shot down over Cuba, and the President's advisers in the Executive Committee were split over what to do.

The solution, urged by several advisers and reflected in the ExComm discussions, was to respond to the first letter as if the second had not arrived. Kennedy's reply accepted the offer of removing the missiles in exchange for a pledge not to invade Cuba. The same evening Robert Kennedy met the Soviet ambassador, Anatoly Dobrynin, privately. He delivered the reply with a warning that time was running out, and he gave an assurance that the Jupiter missiles in Turkey would be removed later, on condition that this part stayed secret.

On 28 October Khrushchev announced on the radio that the missiles would be dismantled. The crisis was over.
lesson: When your counterpart sends mixed signals, answer the one you can work with and give him a way to save face. Not every concession needs to be public.
people: John F. Kennedy, Robert Kennedy, Nikita Khrushchev, Anatoly Dobrynin
source: ExComm meeting transcripts; Robert F. Kennedy, Thirteen Days (1969); Anatoly Dobrynin, In Confidence (1995)
caveat: For years the secret promise on the Turkish missiles was concealed, so early accounts gave the letter tactic more credit than it deserved.
